one_liner: Boost's assembly-backed stackful context switch (fiber, callcc/continuation): about 9 ns per switch versus 547 ns for glibc swapcontext.
what_it_does: Boost.Context gives C++11 code first-class stackful execution contexts: boost::context::fiber (the newer API, reference implementation of P0876) and callcc()/continuation (the older one), each a one-shot, move-only handle that resume() invalidates and replaces. It is the switching layer under Boost.Coroutine2, Boost.Fiber and many coroutine runtimes; you supply or pick a stack allocator (fixedsize_stack, protected_fixedsize_stack with a guard page, pooled_fixedsize_stack, segmented_stack). It is not a drop-in for makecontext/swapcontext: the API is C++ objects, and the backend (fcontext, ucontext or WinFiber) is chosen when the library is built.
how_it_is_fast: The default fcontext_t backend is a hand-written jump_fcontext/make_fcontext/ontop_fcontext routine per architecture, ABI and binary format. On x86-64 SysV it pushes only the callee-saved registers (R12-R15, RBX, RBP) plus MXCSR and the x87 control word onto the current stack, uses the stack pointer itself as the context handle, swaps RSP and jumps to the saved return address; data is passed in registers as a transfer_t. Unlike glibc swapcontext it does not save or restore the signal mask, so no rt_sigprocmask system call happens per switch, which is where most of the 60x gap to the ucontext_t backend comes from (the library's own rationale says ucontext_t is slow because preserving the signal mask needs system calls).
when_to_use: Building coroutines, generators, green threads or a fiber scheduler in C++ where a switch must cost tens of nanoseconds, not a system call.
Replacing makecontext/swapcontext (deprecated in POSIX.1-2004, removed in POSIX.1-2008) in existing code on x86-64, AArch64, ARM, i386, RISC-V64, POWER, MIPS, s390x, SPARC64, LoongArch64 or Alpha.
Asymmetric or symmetric stackful switching where code must suspend from deep inside nested calls, which stackless C++20 coroutines cannot do.
Projects already depending on Boost, or wanting the battle-tested layer that Boost.Fiber and Boost.Coroutine2 use, with pluggable stack allocators and guard pages.
when_not_to_use: Code that relies on a per-context signal mask: fcontext switches do not preserve it (stated in the rationale), only the slow ucontext backend does.

Builds that need AddressSanitizer: sanitizers are supported only with context-impl=ucontext plus BOOST_USE_ASAN, i.e. on the backend that is about 60x slower per the project's table; Valgrind needs valgrind=on and BOOST_USE_VALGRIND.
PPC64 code that keeps live values in floating-point registers across switches: issue #232 (open since 2023, patch offered 2026-08) reports FP14-FP31 are not preserved since about Boost 1.61.

Windows ARM64 with fcontext (b2 defaults that target to WinFiber; issue #336 reports a 16-byte stack-pointer skew in ontop_fcontext that breaks /GS and SEH unwinding), AArch64 builds that require GCS or PAC (issues #332, #338), and WebAssembly/Emscripten (issues #109, #292).
Tiny C or embedded projects that want a single-file switcher without Boost's build system and assembler setup.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (Boost compiled library with per-platform assembly; fiber and continuation front ends are headers)
integration.dependencies: Boost headers (Config, Assert, Core and others); GNU as and the C preprocessor on POSIX, MASM on Windows x86, ARMasm on Windows ARM; the benchmark also links Boost.Chrono and Boost.ProgramOptions
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; documented minimums MSVC 14.0 (VS2015), GCC 4.8, Clang 3.4; b2 or CMake (BOOST_CONTEXT_IMPLEMENTATION, BOOST_CONTEXT_ABI, BOOST_CONTEXT_BINARY_FORMAT cache variables)
integration.platforms: fcontext: x86_64 (SysV/x32 ELF, MS PE, Mach-O), i386, arm/aarch64 (ELF, Mach-O, PE), ppc32/ppc64 (ELF, XCOFF, Mach-O), mips O32/N64, riscv64, s390x, sparc64, loongarch64, alpha; elsewhere ucontext_t or WinFiber fallback
integration.thread_safety: A fiber or continuation runs on one thread at a time and may be migrated to another thread between resumes (README); handles are one-shot and move-only, so no concurrent use of one handle. Not documented further.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces ucontext_t switching only after porting to the fiber or callcc API; the same library can be rebuilt with context-impl=ucontext, so behaviour other than the signal mask matches

gotchas: Harness detail: the 'CPU cycles' column is rdtsc ticks at the TSC's nominal rate, not core cycles (1130/547 = 2.07 and 19/9 = 2.1 ticks per ns, which also points to a 2.1 GHz clock rather than the doc's 2.2 GHz); the ns figures are integer-truncated after dividing by 1,000,000 round trips and by 2, so '9 ns' means 9.0-9.99 ns and the speedup is 55-61x, from one unrepeated run.

Measured through the callcc()/continuation wrapper, not raw jump_fcontext (performance/fcontext exists but is not in the table) and not the newer fiber API; the Windows-Fiber column cannot come from the Linux machine named on the page.

An exception escaping a context-function calls std::terminate; do not switch from inside a catch block; catch(...) handlers must rethrow detail::forced_unwind or destroying an unfinished fiber cannot unwind its stack.

With -fstack-protector define BOOST_CONTEXT_TLS_STACK_PROTECTOR; on Windows with fcontext turn off /GL, use /EHs instead of /EHsc and pass asmflags=\safeseh; issue #327 (open) reports detail/invoke.hpp failing to compile where std::result_of is gone (removed in C++20).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against libco (higan-emu), the only switcher among the siblings, pick Boost.Context when you need a C++ API with stack allocators, guard pages, forced unwinding and a wider ABI list (s390x, LoongArch64, RISC-V64, SPARC64, MIPS, XCOFF) maintained inside Boost; pick libco when you want a tiny C library with no build system. The other siblings are compute kernels, not context switchers.
verified_claims_summary: The project's doc/performance.qbk (about 2017) reports a callcc()/continuation round trip divided by two: 9 ns / 19 TSC ticks per switch with the fcontext_t assembly backend versus 547 ns / 1130 for the same API on the ucontext_t backend (glibc swapcontext), built with gcc-6.3.1 at b2 variant=release optimization=speed on a dual Xeon E5-2620 v4 under Linux; about 55-61x lower latency given the truncated ns figure (derived from page data). The 49 ns Windows-Fiber figure was necessarily measured on another OS.
status_note: Actively maintained (latest commit 2026-10-07, merges through Sept-Oct 2026 adding Alpha support and ASan fixes) and BSL-1.0, but the performance table has not been re-run since the gcc-6.3.1 era, and several platform assembly bugs (PPC64 FP registers #232, Windows ARM64 ontop SP skew #336) are open without maintainer fixes.
